cards.tip: FIX — When your customer mentioned the room was still 90 degrees after trying a window unit, that's when you present 3-4 options with clear pricing—compressor replacement, compressor plus upgrade package, full system—then ask directly which one works best instead of staying in tech-explanation mode.

FIX — When the husband said he didn't want to do it at $500, Chris should have asked 'Is that the price, or are you unsure if the filters are needed?' instead of just offering to get estimates — a clarifying question would've let him either present a smaller starter option or resell the $2-3k motor-failure consequence.

WIN — When Nancy asked "what is the membership," you immediately converted abstract benefits into concrete math on their repair: "$950 becomes $807 with 15% off, saves you $140 right now"—that specific dollar amount tied to their exact problem closed both the repair and enrollment.

FIX — Your inspection plan was solid, but once you found the issue, you needed to explain it to Julius in plain terms, present 4+ repair and upgrade options with specific pricing, and ask directly for the sale—he'd already signaled urgency by saying it's gotten much worse.

FIX — The customer trusted you to check the attic after they mentioned past issues—at that moment, you should have said 'I'll come back with 4-6 different repair and upgrade options so you can pick what makes sense,' not just a single fix.

WIN — When the family pushed back on the $548 labor, you negotiated down to $448 while validating their emergency (heat wave with kids and elderly in the house) and immediately committed to calling your boss for expedited ordering—that combination of fairness, empathy, and concrete action converted their hesitation into a signed approval.

WIN — When Juan said 'everything is up and cooling, my man' and set the clear expectation 'by the time nighttime, like you guys are ready to go to bed, everything should be good and go,' the customer had proof the repair worked and immediate confidence to approve the work.

WIN — When the customer said 'so it's borderline' on the motor starter voltage, you explained exactly what happens when it's underpowered—the compressor can't start properly—and they immediately approved the $224 replacement; consequence-focused explanations close objections.

FIX — After diagnosing the zone sensor and compressor issues, Adrian should have presented 3-4 repair options with clear pricing and asked directly for the business instead of pivoting to 'Can I get any water?' without discussing what comes next or how much it costs.

FIX — When the customer said they had one unit down out of seven, that was your moment to say: 'I'll check this one first and your others, it'll take about 30 minutes, then I'll show you repair options and pricing'—instead the conversation drifted to personal topics, and you never built or presented upgrade options or asked for the sale.

FIX — When the customer said they'd already bought filters from Costco, you needed to say 'Perfect, let me show you what else we can address today' and present 3-4 alternatives with pricing (coil cleaning, duct sealing, thermostat upgrade); instead the call drifted into personal conversation, and the specific move lost was translating your technical findings into a customer value menu.

FIX — Customer said 'we have some ground for negotiation' because they can't sleep in the heat — you responded 'it's out of my control' instead of asking directly for the sale: should have been 'let's get the supervisor scheduled tomorrow morning to get you fixed, can I book that?'
FIX — Transcript cuts off before diagnosis findings and close; welcome set strong expectations, but we can't assess if you identified issues, built upgrade value, and directly asked for the sale.

WIN — You diagnosed the burnt switch as a fire hazard and when the customer mentioned their wife's fire concerns, you said 'I'd rather it turn off as an indicator... because something, something like that causes fires' — validating their worry and making the $438 repair an instant approval.
WIN — Your confident 'I can ask him, and more than likely he'll say yeah' showed the customer you'd fight for them—delivering the $100 discount to $700 earned instant approval.

FIX — When the customer said 'We're on fixed income, so we'll think about it,' directly connecting the soft start cost to the compressor replacement cost ('if that compressor fails, you're looking at $3,000; this $1,351 investment protects it and saves energy') would have reframed the value and likely closed the sale.
WIN — You showed the worn contacts with carbon buildup, quoted $400–425 with parts ready, and the customer approved on the spot—that diagnostic clarity combined with execution readiness wins sales.
FIX — Jose needs to return from the inspection with specific findings, present multiple repair and upgrade options with clear pricing, and ask directly for the customer's authorization.

FIX — When the customer asked to separate the soft start kit estimate from the capacitor work, you had a window to close—ask directly: 'Want me to go ahead and install those today?' instead of saying you'd put an estimate together and walking away.

FIX — When the customer signaled she wanted Sierra to supply and install all four Nests with the extended warranty through the maintenance program, Matt should have confirmed the sale immediately with "Perfect — so we'll do all four Nests with the maintenance program. Let me confirm pricing and we're good to go" instead of stepping out to get estimates without locking in the commitment first.

FIX — when the customer was crystal clear 'that noise gotta go,' you should have presented repair and upgrade options (warranty compressor replacement, premium quiet model) instead of deferring to your manager—that's the moment to build value and ask for the sale.

FIX — Set clear expectations at the start of the visit so customers know what to expect: when the customer mentioned the clicking sounds, that was your opening to say, 'I'll definitely check that out. Let me grab my tools and do a full diagnostic—should take about 15 minutes—and then I'll walk you through what we found and your repair options.'

FIX — You diagnosed the shroud vibration quickly and positioned the soft start upgrade well for the 5-year-old unit. Ask directly: "Let me get you set up with the soft start" instead of leaving it conditional—that converts interest into a yes.

WIN — Corey's diagnosis of the recurring starter failures and over-amping across all units in the context of Las Vegas heat stress convinced the customer the repair was necessary; they approved the $1,381 minimum package without hesitation, confirming the diagnosis earned their trust.

FIX — When the customer mentioned hidden problems, offer the SAM maintenance agreement right then instead of waiting for your options presentation. Without that early framing, your repair options feel like separate line items, not a cohesive solution. Lead with membership so it ties everything together for a stronger close.

WIN — You completed the filter change and earned genuine warmth, confirming good rapport—when you noted 'I see you guys change pretty often... the 3 inches is so much better,' you had the perfect opening to pitch the SAM membership or premium filter upgrade, but you left without asking; next time, close on a membership offer when the customer shows they care for their system.

FIX — When the customer worried about signal loss and you mentioned you've had to replace devices like theirs before, that's when to offer a preventive maintenance or monitoring plan instead of 'call me if it happens again'—you identified the pain but didn't sell the solution to prevent it.

FIX — when the customer said 'I'll get that next time' about the 3-inch filters after you explained they last longer, that was your close moment—instead of deferring to email, offer 'I have those available, let me install one today' to capture the upgrade immediately.

FIX — When the customer raised cost concerns and mentioned needing landlord approval, present your repair options with specific pricing ($X base repair / $Y with soft start upgrade) immediately so they can request approval instead of waiting for the full diagnostic.

FIX — When your homeowner said she'd grab filters from the closet, instead of accepting that, present the complete package with urgency: 'Filters alone won't solve it—the dirty coil is restricting cooling too, and together they're running your compressor at 130 amps instead of 120; here's the full protection plan we recommend,' then ask for approval.

FIX — When the customer said the system is 'working fine' and you noticed they use it a lot, that was your opening to ask what matters most to them (efficiency, extended warranty, preventative maintenance)—build 4+ upgrade options with specific pricing during your inspection instead of jumping to the membership offer that got declined.

WIN — Customer said they only had $1,000, and you gave them '$150 for the part. $16 for the first payment'—that exact match to their budget, combined with your credibility (soft-start story, maintenance philosophy), made the sale feel safe and they closed immediately.

FIX — When the customer asked if the compressor was covered by warranty, that opened the door to build more options around their budget—extended warranties, seasonal maintenance bundled with the repair, or financing—but you presented only two technical paths instead; more distinct choices would have made the hard start one legitimate option among several rather than a second-class compromise.

WIN — Your diagnosis of the burnt voltage switch was stellar; combining that expertise with 'I'm going to waive that $79 fee' for membership signup was the closer—the customer immediately confirmed the prices and approved both the repair and membership.
WIN — When the customer hesitated on the $516 surge protectors, you connected the maintenance plan's 15% discount to today's purchases, turning that price objection into an approved upgrade.

FIX — Your opening should frame the visit before diagnosis—tell the customer what you'll check, roughly how long, and what happens if you find an issue—this prepares them to hear and decide on options later.

WIN — You walked through the parts inventory (housing, motor, cage), confirmed prior diagnosis was understood, and got agreement to proceed with the blower motor replacement; the customer's confidence came from your methodical setup review and reassurance that you'd handle everything correctly.
Review for coaching insights.
FIX — Customer committed to filter upgrade, creating perfect moment to directly ask for membership; tech instead deferred decision, losing urgency and a two-year revenue commitment.

WIN — Customer's wife had already qualified for financing before Fabian arrived, removing the financial objection; Fabian capitalized by efficiently diagnosing the TXV metering device issue and presenting it as an upgrade option while securing approval for the primary compressor repair.
Review for coaching insights.
WIN — when customer hesitated on $1,044 cost, Corey shifted focus to compressor damage risk ($14,000 system loss) to make the repair protective rather than expensive.

FIX — You built strong rapport and explained the diagnostic findings, but stopped short of a direct close; when the customer showed interest in protecting against future breakdowns, you should have said 'Let's get you on the membership plan today so you never have to worry about this again' instead of leaving them to 'think about it.'
Review for coaching insights.

FIX — You repaired the condenser fan motor under warranty ($272) and got paid, but the customer had been without cooling for three nights. When they said "We didn't sleep almost three nights," acknowledge the hardship and use it as a hook: offer the membership as insurance against future emergencies (free emergency visit included).

WIN — Customer hadn't slept in 3 nights. You diagnosed the stuck damper motor, explained the lifetime warranty covered parts, and presented labor cost ($338) clearly. Customer approved immediately when you showed the root cause with video evidence and confirmed she'd feel relief "as soon as you walk in."
FIX — Customer revealed previous $500 bill from another tech's repair; opportunity to offer preventive maintenance plan was missed, then tech ended call before presenting solutions.

FIX — You thoroughly diagnosed prior service history and explained parts availability, but when the customer expressed concerns about cost or prior work, you didn't proactively build a value case showing what coverage they'd get under a maintenance membership—a direct ask with that tied to their past frustration would have moved them to 'yes.'

WIN — Corey methodically diagnosed a tricky partial capacitor failure affecting only compressor side, clearly explained the technical issue, and secured the customer on the maintenance program while solving the repair.

FIX — When the customer said 'forget it' to the soft start device price, you pivoted to the microprocessor option, but you didn't pause to ask 'Are you prioritizing preventing future failures or reducing noise?'—understanding their true motivation would have helped you close at least one of the two upgrade paths.

WIN — Tech showed burnt voltage switch, explained steel-on-steel grinding and $6,000-$8,000 compressor replacement cost, then presented clear upgrade options, driving customer to commit immediately.
FIX — Customer expressed compressor concern directly; tech confirmed diagnosis but didn't pause to quote repair/replacement costs or present options before leaving for tools.

WIN — Jose discovered fan motor leaking oil and burnt voltage switch during thorough inspection. He presented 4 distinct options: fan motor ($372), voltage switch ($433), microprocessor upgrade ($516), and filter replacement. Customer committed to fan motor after Jose explained oil leak severity and December 3 warranty expiration—the deadline created urgency for this high-value close.

FIX — You did excellent work explaining the motor starter failure and presenting both the straight repair ($557) and membership-discounted option ($490 plus 2-year coverage), but when the customer hesitated on price, you didn't ask a confirming question like 'If we can work out payments, does the 2-year protection make sense?'—that follow-up close might have sealed it.

FIX — When you identified the clogged filters and fan schedule issue, the customer opened a door to accept your recommendations; you should have consolidated that into 2-3 specific packages (maintenance plan with different service tiers) and asked directly for a commitment rather than just offering a single membership pitch.

WIN — You built enough diagnostic credibility that 'would you like to get them changed?' got an immediate yes from Sergio; next time offer SAM membership at that same moment while the customer is already buying.

WIN — When the customer vented about a past no-show appointment and poor phone service, you owned the problem specifically ('I'm pretty sure they're not there with us no more') and repositioned the visit as your commitment to five-star service — that accountability and empathy moved them from frustrated to signing up same-day.

WIN — Fabian delivered exceptional technical education explaining why soft start doesn't fix running noise, identified vibration/damping as the real issue, and built customer confidence through clear diagnostics.

FIX — Chris said 'if you continue to have the problem, give us a call' instead of directly asking: 'The switch is showing early wear signs—let's replace it today while I'm here to prevent a shutdown.'

FIX — You explained the membership benefits clearly, but when the customer wasn't ready to commit, you handed them the brochure to 'think about it'—reminding them that they'd already had one major failure and positioning the plan as protection would have been a more direct close: 'Since you've had that battery issue, this plan means you'll never pay for emergency trips again—ready to get you set up?'
